findings.claim: Updates overwrite sessions.json and findings.json in place, so interruption can destroy previously committed history; an empty findings file is subsequently treated as an empty new store.
findings.trigger: A process crash, termination, or I/O failure occurs after WriteAllText truncates an existing JSON store but before the complete replacement is written.

evidence.observation: Write-JsonFile delegates directly to File.WriteAllText on the destination. There is no temporary-file replacement or backup. Read-FindingsFile returns New-FindingsStore when the existing file reads as empty.
Writing sessions last does not protect either file against interruption within its own overwrite, and orphan detection cannot reconstruct overwritten history.

findings.verification: In an isolated fixture with existing history, inject termination immediately after destination truncation during each store update, then restart and inspect whether all previously committed records remain recoverable.
findings.remedy: Serialize and flush to a temporary file in the same directory, replace the destination atomically using an appropriate platform primitive, and retain recovery data. Treat empty or unreadable existing stores as corruption rather than new state.

findings.claim: Stale-lock reclamation can delete a newly acquired replacement lock because checking ownership and deleting the path are not atomic.
findings.trigger: Two processes inspect the same stale lock and both complete the final reread before either deletes it; one then replaces the stale lock before the other executes File.Delete.

evidence.observation: CreateNew is atomic, but its handle is closed immediately. Reclamation compares text, closes the read handle, and subsequently deletes by path. Release likewise checks the nonce separately from deletion.
After both checks succeed, contender A can acquire its new lock before contender B deletes the path. B can then acquire another lock while A continues, defeating the single-writer guarantee.

findings.verification: Use barriers around the stale-lock reread and deletion in an isolated concurrency harness to force this interleaving; assert that at most one contender reaches ledger loading.
findings.remedy: Use an ownership mechanism held for the entire critical section with platform-appropriate exclusion, or serialize reclamation with a separate reliable guard. Do not rely on reread-then-delete as conditional deletion.

findings.claim: Recovery does not detect or reserve consultation numbers belonging only to persisted reviewer checks, allowing a later consultation to reuse a number and misattribute the earlier check; Raw mode also ignores orphan finding-source reservations.
findings.trigger: Consultation N adds reviewer_checks to existing findings without creating new findings, persists findings.json, and crashes before sessions.json is updated; the next consultation allocates N again.

evidence.observation: Number allocation examines ledger entries and finding source.consult only. Reviewer checks contain their own consult numbers but are not scanned. List determines orphan status from each finding's original source, and Raw mode does not read findings.json.

The original finding can still match its committed source entry, hiding the orphan check. A subsequent ledger entry using the same number makes the old check appear associated with a different consultation. Reply-only orphans are also outside List's scan.

findings.verification: Seed a committed finding, persist a checks-only consultation, interrupt before the sessions write, then run List and another consultation; verify orphan detection and that the consultation number is not reused, including a Raw rerun.
findings.remedy: Persist a consultation reservation or pending receipt before execution, detect incomplete consultations independently of new findings, and account for every audit reference when allocating numbers. Apply reservation rules in Raw mode too.

findings.claim: The revision fingerprint does not distinguish executable-mode changes when file content and porcelain status remain unchanged.
findings.trigger: On a filesystem with executable modes and Git mode tracking enabled, toggle the executable bit of an already content-modified tracked file; both states retain porcelain status ' M' and the same content blob.

evidence.observation: Manifest entries contain XY, path, rename source, and a content blob or directory/deletion sentinel. They do not contain the file mode.
Both states serialize to the same manifest despite differing execution behavior, defeating the design-review requirement to include types and modes.

findings.verification: In a disposable Unix repository with core.filemode=true, modify a tracked script, fingerprint it, toggle its executable bit without changing content, and compare fingerprints.
findings.remedy: Include the relevant file type and executable mode in each manifest entry, with explicit coverage rules for symlinks and platforms without mode tracking.

findings.remedy: Hash these inputs under the acquired lock and rehash them after the review, recording drift independently of source-tree drift; immutable input copies would provide stronger binding.

findings.claim: Task ownership can be released or reclaimed while the prior Codex process is still running.
findings.trigger: Timeout termination reports surviving descendants, or the bridge process dies while its separately launched Codex child survives.

evidence.observation: Known survivors change only the failure message; finally still releases the lock. Stale ownership is decided solely from the bridge PID and start time, without proving its child tree has stopped.
A subsequent invocation can resume the same thread or mutate task state while the earlier Codex invocation remains active.

findings.verification: In an isolated harness, force termination failure for one descendant and separately terminate only the bridge parent; verify that a second consultation cannot acquire ownership while the old child remains active.
findings.remedy: Supervise the child tree with an appropriate job/process-group lifetime mechanism. Preserve a recovery/quarantine state when termination cannot be confirmed, rather than unconditionally unlocking or treating the parent's death as sufficient.

findings.claim: Lock acquisition destructively replaces the previous recovery record before validating or durably transferring its reservation and child information, so another crash can erase a reserved consultation number or a surviving-child quarantine.
findings.trigger: A previous run leaves a reservation or live-child record; a consultation or status updater acquires the handle and crashes after Write-LockRecord replaces that record but before the old record is consumed or restored. Interruption during the in-place truncation is another loss window.

evidence.observation: The new record initializes n and child_pid to null, nn to empty, and survivors to an empty array. Enter-TaskLock writes it at line 1542 before parsing the previous text or checking previous children. The old information exists only in memory during that interval.
Write-LockRecord truncates the held file before rewriting it. The status updater restores a previous reservation only on normal finally execution.

evidence.reference: Memory-only Write-LockRecord probe using a stream adapter
evidence.observation: Replacing a record containing n=9, nn=20, child_pid=12345 and survivors with the acquisition record produced null reservation/child fields and an empty survivors array. No filesystem writes were performed.

evidence.reference: Crash between replacement and previous-record validation
evidence.observation: After that crash, the next invocation cannot recover the erased reservation or detect the previously recorded live child. Correct scanning of persisted reviewer checks does not recover a reservation that had no other durable reference.

findings.verification: In an isolated fixture, seed an uncommitted reservation and a live-child quarantine separately, pause acquisition immediately after the replacement write, kill the acquiring process, and verify that the next invocation still preserves the reservation and refuses the live child.
findings.remedy: Separate the permanent ownership lock from atomically persisted recovery metadata. Validate the previous record before changing it, transfer reservations durably, preserve quarantine until child termination is established, and refuse corrupt recovery metadata rather than treating it as absent.

findings.claim: The Unix release path can split task ownership across an unlinked lock inode and a newly created lock file because it deletes the pathname used for descriptor-based exclusion.
findings.trigger: A contender opens the existing lock inode and pauses before acquiring its advisory lock; the owner unlinks and closes it; that contender then acquires the old inode while another invocation creates and locks the pathname's replacement.

evidence.observation: The documented Unix mechanism is advisory flock through FileShare.None. Acquisition opens the pathname, while release unlinks that pathname before disposing the held stream.

A descriptor already referring to the old inode is not redirected to the replacement pathname. Under the stated descriptor-locking mechanism, the two contenders can therefore lock different files for the same task.

findings.verification: On a supported Unix runtime, use an instrumented opener or syscall barriers to pause a contender between opening the old lock file and acquiring its lock, release the owner, start another contender, and assert that simultaneous ownership is impossible.
findings.remedy: Keep the ownership lock file permanently at a stable pathname and inode; release ownership by closing the handle rather than unlinking it. Store recoverable run metadata separately.

findings.claim: Artifact after-hashing selects paths case-insensitively, so case-distinct artifacts can be bound to the wrong after-review bytes and an actual artifact change can go undetected.

evidence.reference: Memory-only reproduction of the artifactItems lookup
evidence.observation: With a.bin mapped to lower and A.bin mapped to upper, the exact lookup selected lower as the rehash target for both artifacts.

evidence.reference: Initially equal artifact hashes followed by an uppercase-path-only edit
evidence.observation: Both after hashes can still equal the initial hash because the unchanged lowercase file is read twice, leaving artifacts_changed_during_review false.

findings.verification: In a case-sensitive fixture, supply two case-distinct artifacts with identical initial contents, modify only the second during a delayed review, and verify its own sha256_after changes and artifact drift is reported.
findings.remedy: Carry each artifact's resolved full path alongside its initial hash and rehash that exact object, or use an ordinal case-sensitive lookup without selecting the first case-insensitive match.

findings.claim: The intentional fallback can prevent automatic recovery indefinitely while unrelated matching Codex processes remain present; this is an accepted, documented availability tradeoff.
findings.trigger: An interrupted pending record exists and an unrelated long-lived or continuously overlapping Codex-looking process started after that record matches the fallback.

evidence.observation: Fallback matching does not establish task identity, has no age cutoff, and refuses while a match exists. The README documents the limitation and deliberate pending-record clearance.
A matching process without a recorded parent relationship produced Active=true and a refusal explicitly labelled 'task not verifiable'.

findings.verification: In an isolated recovery fixture, confirm an unrelated matching process causes a labelled refusal and that recovery succeeds after the match disappears.
findings.remedy: Accept as the documented operational limitation; retain explicit manual clearance after process inspection with task writers stopped. No release-blocking code change is required.
